strengths: Provides a comprehensive and well-organized theoretical taxonomy of RLHF vs. DPO performance gaps across seven model-misspecification conditions (Figure 1), meaningfully extending prior work (Nika et al. 2024, Swamy et al. 2025) by removing the realizability assumption and analyzing fine-grained cases.

The statistical separation result in Section 4 (Theorems 10/11) is a novel and interesting contribution: it rigorously shows that RLHF's two-stage reward learning can exploit sparsity in the ground-truth reward (achieving O(k log d/n) error) while DPO's implicit reward learning cannot (Ω(d/n) lower bound), giving a concrete mechanism for RLHF's practical sample efficiency advantage.

The token-level analysis connecting the policy's implicit q*/soft-value function to the reward model's simpler target (Section 3, 'Curse of value function') offers useful intuition for why policy models are more prone to misspecification than reward models of the same scale.

Controlled experiments (Section 5.1) on GPT-2-Large with PKU-SafeRLHF closely track the theoretical predictions across all four misspecification conditions, and the paper further strengthens external validity by mapping its propositions onto results from several independent large-scale empirical studies (Section 5.2), which is a valuable synthesis effort.

Extensive, mostly rigorous appendix proofs for the main propositions and theorems, including explicit bandit constructions, and a thoughtful discussion connecting the theory to alternative preference-modeling objectives (Appendix A) beyond the BT model.
weaknesses: Several key claims (Propositions 4 and 7, concerning online DPO under policy/double misspecification) are only verified numerically rather than proven analytically, weakening the rigor of what are presented as central results in Figure 1.

Most separation results are of the form 'there exists an environment such that...', established via small, stylized constructions (e.g., 3-action bandits, specific feature mappings satisfying contrived algebraic relations, a two-token duplicated-preference DTSP task). These existence proofs establish possibility rather than typicality, and it is unclear how representative such constructions are of realistic LLM training regimes.

The paper's scope is very broad (7 misspecification conditions, two distinct theoretical regimes, plus a bonus appendix on alternative reward modeling), which, combined with dense notation and long derivations, makes the manuscript difficult to parse and assess in full; some sections (e.g., Conditions 6/7, 'no consistent gap') yield limited actionable conclusions beyond 'it depends on reward quality'.

Empirical validation is confined to a single small-scale model (GPT-2-Large, 774M) and a single dataset (PKU-SafeRLHF), which the authors acknowledge as a limitation; while the connection to external large-scale studies partially compensates, the controlled experiments themselves provide only qualitative, not quantitative, confirmation of the theory.

The choice of the regularized value function as the performance metric (versus the unregularized metric used in the most directly comparable prior work, Nika et al. 2024) is defended but still complicates apples-to-apples comparison with that literature, and the paper's own statistical results (Theorem 15) require restrictive assumptions (e.g., n = Ω̃(d²) for the DPO lower bound, well-conditioned Gram matrix spectrum) that may not hold in practice.

strengths: The paper provides a broad and reasonably systematic taxonomy of RLHF vs. DPO performance comparisons across seven mis-specification conditions (no mis-specification, policy-only, reward-only, double mis-specification with isomorphic/relatively-stronger reward or policy classes), each supported by formal propositions and constructive proofs.

The statistical-efficiency analysis in Section 4 (dual-token sparse prediction task) is a concrete and technically careful contribution: it rigorously separates the sample complexity of reward learning (which can exploit sparsity, achieving O(k log d/n)) from DPO's surrogate reward learning (stuck at Omega(d/n)), using established sparse-recovery machinery adapted to the preference-learning setting.

The paper connects its theoretical claims to a reasonable number of existing large-scale empirical studies (Razin et al., Swamy et al., Xu et al., Ivison et al., Rafailov et al.), which helps ground the otherwise abstract theory in practically observed phenomena.

Small-scale controlled experiments (GPT-2-Large on PKU-SafeRLHF) are explicitly designed to instantiate each theoretical condition and largely track the qualitative predictions, providing an internally consistent story between theory and experiment.

The related-work positioning relative to Nika et al. (2024) and Swamy et al. (2025) is explicit and the paper correctly identifies how it extends/differs from the most relevant prior work (regularized vs. unregularized value, finer-grained mis-specification analysis, improved/contrasted statistical rates).

Appendix A offers an interesting auxiliary discussion connecting the policy-gradient-consistent reward objective to existing alternatives (IPO, PILAF), adding some conceptual value beyond the main propositions.
weaknesses: Many of the central results are existence-type propositions proved via highly engineered toy constructions (e.g., 3-action bandits with specifically chosen feature vectors that make one reward identical to a constant under the model class), which demonstrate that a gap *can* occur but provide little insight into how common, large, or representative such gaps are in realistic settings with large vocabularies and neural parameterizations.

The most practically relevant setting -- double model mis-specification with non-isomorphic classes (Conditions 6 and 7) -- yields an inconclusive 'no consistent gap, depends on reward quality' result, which undercuts the paper's stated goal of giving 'practical insights into when each method is preferred,' since this is arguably the regime closest to real-world deployment (reward model smaller than policy model, both imperfect).

The statistical separation result (Theorem 10/11) is derived under a narrow, specifically constructed Dual-Token Sparse Prediction task with strong assumptions (token duplication, well-conditioned spectrum, specific feature mapping linking the two tokens); it is unclear how this generalizes beyond this constructed scenario to realistic multi-token generation with rich token-level dependencies.

Experiments are conducted only on a small GPT-2-Large (774M) model with a single dataset (PKU-SafeRLHF); the 'verification' experiments are essentially constructed to match the preconditions of each proposition (freezing layers to induce policy mis-specification, replacing projection matrices to induce reward mis-specification), which makes the experiments closer to engineered confirmations than independent empirical tests of the theory's predictive power.

The connections to existing large-scale empirical literature in Section 5.2 are somewhat selective (single tables/figures cited per paper) without deeper engagement on whether the cited empirical gaps are actually driven by the specific mechanism (representation mis-specification) the theory isolates, versus other confounds (optimization instability, hyperparameters, data scale) present in those studies.

The paper is extremely dense with notation and many propositions/conditions, several proved only numerically (Propositions 4 and 7) rather than analytically, which weakens the rigor of claims that are prominently featured in the main text (e.g., 'online DPO cannot close the gap' and 'online DPO can outperform both RLHF and DPO').

Limitations discussion is thin (two bullet points) and does not address the generalizability concerns above, e.g., whether the linear/log-linear token-level parameterization assumptions meaningfully approximate transformer-based reward/policy models used in practice.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive, fine-grained theoretical decomposition of the RLHF vs. DPO performance gap into explicit (model mis-specification) and implicit (statistical/sample-efficiency) sources, going beyond the common realizability assumption used in most prior theoretical work.

The exact-optimization analysis is thorough and systematic: it enumerates essentially all combinations of reward/policy model mis-specification (Conditions 1-7), gives explicit propositions for each, and backs up abstract claims with concrete constructive counterexamples (e.g., multi-armed bandit constructions in Appendix B.3-B.9) rather than relying purely on asymptotic arguments.

The finite-sample analysis (Section 4, Theorem 10/11) is a nice technical contribution: it carefully constructs a token-level linear parameterization (DTSP task) in which the reward is sparse but the induced DPO/q-function target is dense, yielding a rigorous statistical separation (Ω(d/n) for DPO vs O(k log d/n) for RLHF with sparse reward recovery), building on and generalizing existing sparse-recovery results (Yao et al. 2025) to a 'relative' estimator setting needed for this comparison.

The paper connects its theoretical predictions to controlled small-scale experiments (Figures 2-4) that qualitatively match each proposition, and further cross-validates against six independent published large-scale empirical studies (Table/Figure citations from Razin et al., Swamy et al., Xu et al., Ivison et al., Rafailov et al.), which strengthens the practical relevance and believability of the theory.

The related work discussion is unusually careful and specific, explicitly contrasting with the closest prior work (Nika et al. 2024, Swamy et al. 2025) and precisely stating what is novel/improved (regularized vs. unregularized value metric, extension beyond isomorphic case, sharper statistical rates under sparsity).

The appendix bonus section (Appendix A) offers a thoughtful additional perspective connecting the policy-induced 'real' reward objective, MLE, and PILAF/online sampling, and sketches alternative objectives (online IPO) as a forward-looking discussion, showing depth beyond the main results.
weaknesses: Proposition 4 and Proposition 7, two of the more striking claims (online DPO cannot close the gap under policy mis-specification; online DPO can beat RLHF under isomorphism), are only established via a single numerical/constructive example rather than a general proof, which limits confidence in how broadly these conclusions generalize beyond the specific handcrafted bandit instances.

Many of the exact-optimization results rely on small, hand-constructed 3-action bandit/linear-feature counterexamples; while sufficient to prove existence of a gap (as intended by the 'there exists an environment' style propositions), this leaves open how large or representative these gaps are in realistic LLM settings, and the paper's own experiments are run only on a single small GPT-2-Large model and one dataset (PKU-SafeRLHF), raising reproducibility/generality concerns about whether the qualitative ordering would hold at scale or on other preference distributions.

The headline claim that 'RLHF requires significantly fewer samples than DPO' rests on a very specific dual-token sparse-prediction (DTSP) construction with an artificial duplication of the token into the response (Assumption 13: the second token is forced to equal the first), which is a fairly contrived data-generating assumption that may not reflect realistic language generation; the authors themselves acknowledge the parameterization/estimators are 'specific and tailored for the task.'

Section 4's statistical comparison compares an idealized sparse reward estimator (with oracle knowledge of sparsity level k, or tuned ℓ1 regularization) against a vanilla MLE-based DPO estimator; it does not consider whether DPO-side regularization or structure-aware policy parameterizations could close part of this gap, which could overstate the generality of the separation.

Although the paper lists multiple empirical cross-validations in Section 5.2, these are qualitative pattern-matching exercises (citing a single table or figure of each external paper to 'support' a particular proposition) rather than controlled validations under the same experimental protocol, so the strength of this evidence is weaker than it may first appear.

The practical actionability of the double mis-specification result (Condition 4: 'no consistent performance gap... depends on the qualities of the reward models') is somewhat limited, since it is the most practically relevant regime (neither model class perfectly captures ground truth) yet yields the least decisive guidance for practitioners choosing between RLHF and DPO.

Presentation issues: the paper is very dense with many conditions/propositions, several of which are proven only in the appendix; the main text would benefit from clearer synthesis of practical takeaways, and some mathematical notation (e.g., stop-gradient operator, difference operator) is introduced but could be streamlined for readability.

strengths: Provides a fairly comprehensive and rigorous theoretical taxonomy (Table 1) of RLHF vs. DPO performance under all four combinations of reward/policy model mis-specification, extending prior isomorphic-class results (Swamy et al. 2026) and improving statistical bounds from Nika et al. (2024).

The dual-token sparse prediction (DTSP) construction in Section 4 gives a clean, quantitative statistical separation (Ω(d/n) for DPO vs O~(k log d/n) for RLHF with sparse rewards), supported by rigorous proofs leveraging compressed-sensing-style sparse-recovery machinery, and is a genuinely novel, concrete contribution.

Theorem 2 and the PILAF-sampler analysis offer an interesting objective-level (rather than gradient-level) characterization of how online DPO approximates the true value function, with a clear second-order-deviation failure mode tied to reward scale, which is empirically corroborated (Figure 1).

The token-level q*-function argument (Section 3, 'curse of value function') gives an intuitive, practically relevant explanation for why policy models generally need larger capacity than reward models, connecting theory to a widely observed empirical practice.

Appendix B provides a constructive/diagnostic view relating the DPO/RLHF MLE gradients to an idealized ℓ2 pairwise-difference objective, naturally explaining the design of online/PILAF samplers and pointing to alternative loss designs (e.g., online IPO).

The paper cross-validates its qualitative predictions against a fairly large number of existing large-scale empirical studies (Table listing 6 papers), in addition to its own small controlled GPT-2-Large experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF, giving some external validity to the theoretical claims.

Extensive, mostly self-contained proofs are provided in the appendix, and the related-work comparison to Nika et al. (2024) and Swamy et al. (2026) is specific and clarifies incremental contributions.
weaknesses: Many central results (Propositions 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9) are existence-type claims ('there exists an environment such that...') established via small, hand-crafted toy bandits (2-3 actions, specific linear feature maps chosen to force the desired inequality). This demonstrates possibility but not typicality, and gives limited predictive/practical guidance about which regime a real system is actually in.

The 'Double Model Mis-specification' analysis (Condition 4, the most realistic regime in practice) largely concludes 'it depends on reward model qualities,' which, while honest, is a fairly weak takeaway relative to the paper's stated goal of guiding practitioners on when to prefer RLHF vs. DPO.

Experiments are conducted only on GPT-2-Large (774M) with very short training (3 iterations for online experiments, 3 seeds), which limits confidence that the qualitative trends will hold at the scale where RLHF/DPO choices actually matter in practice (e.g., billion-to-hundred-billion parameter models as motivated in the introduction).

The DTSP sparse-reward construction, while rigorous, is quite specific (duplicated dual-token responses, fixed θ1 constraint, particular feature decomposition) and the paper acknowledges the main theorems do not extend beyond two tokens; the claimed generality of the 'curse of value function' intuition for multi-token, nonlinear settings is asserted rather than proven.

The connections to existing large-scale empirical studies (Section 5.2) are presented as a list of one-line correspondences without deeper quantitative or causal engagement, which risks being read as selective/confirmatory rather than a rigorous validation.

The paper is extremely dense with heavy notation and many propositions/conditions; despite the appendix table of contents, the main text presentation could be difficult for readers to parse the practical upshot without working through the appendix.

The impact/limitations statement is minimal and mostly procedural; the paper does not discuss potential risks of practitioners over-generalizing from toy constructive counterexamples to real-world deployment decisions.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and under-explored question: characterizing exactly when RLHF outperforms DPO (and vice versa) once the common realizability assumption is dropped. This fills a clear gap relative to prior work (Swamy et al., Nika et al.) that mostly assumes realizability or only handles special linear cases.

The taxonomy in Table 1 (four combinations of reward/policy model misspecification, plus the isomorphic/stronger-reward/stronger-policy sub-cases) is a clean organizing framework, and each cell is backed by an explicit proposition with a constructive proof (mostly small bandit examples), which at least makes the claims falsifiable and verifiable.

The approximate-optimization analysis (Section 4, Theorems 10–11) gives a concrete, if narrow, construction (dual-token sparse prediction task) showing a genuine statistical separation (Ω(d/n) for DPO vs O(k log d /n) for sparse RLHF reward learning) using established sparse-recovery machinery, which is a legitimate technical contribution beyond prior Θ(d/n) vs Θ(√(d/n)) comparisons.

The paper makes a real effort to connect its theoretical cases to existing large-scale empirical papers (Section 5.2) and to run its own small controlled experiments (Section 5.1) that qualitatively track the theoretical predictions across all four misspecification conditions.

Appendix B offers a plausible explanation for why the PILAF/online sampler helps align the DPO objective with the true value function via a Taylor-expansion argument, connecting several recent algorithmic proposals under one lens.
weaknesses: Most of the 'dichotomy' results are existence results built on hand-crafted, low-dimensional (often 3-action, 2-token) bandit constructions with specifically engineered feature maps (e.g., ψ(a3)=½ψ(a1)+½ψ(a2)) chosen precisely to break one method or another. This repeatedly demonstrates 'there exists an environment such that...' rather than establishing which regime is typical or likely in realistic LLM settings, undermining the claimed 'practical insights into when each method is preferred' promised in the abstract.

The overall message across Section 3 is essentially 'it depends on model class and reward quality,' which, while honest, provides limited actionable guidance; several conditions (6 and 7) conclude with 'either method can outperform the other depending on the environment' with no characterization of which situations are common in practice.

The statistical separation result (Theorem 10/11) is derived for a very specific, artificial 'Dual-token sparse prediction' task with duplicated tokens and an explicit θ1=e1 constraint; the authors themselves admit the proof does not extend beyond two tokens, raising doubts about relevance to real autoregressive generation with hundreds/thousands of tokens.

The controlled experiments are small-scale (GPT-2-Large, 3 seeds) and the 'weak reward'/'weak policy' conditions are created by artificially freezing specific layers or replacing projection heads — an operationalization that may not reflect how capacity gaps actually arise in practice (e.g., the 6B vs 175B disparity motivated in the introduction is never actually tested).

Section 5.2's mapping of theoretical propositions onto specific tables/figures in six different external papers is largely anecdotal pattern-matching (citing a single table or figure as 'supporting' a proposition) rather than a systematic or quantitative validation, and risks over-claiming generality from cherry-picked instances.

Theorem 2's bound involves a second-order Taylor remainder that can become 'substantial' or cause 'divergence' under exactly the misspecified conditions that are the paper's main focus, weakening confidence in the online-DPO approximation claims precisely where they are most needed.

The writing is extremely dense and notation-heavy, with most substantive proofs deferred to a ~27-page appendix; the main text often states results with minimal intuition, making the paper hard to parse and assess without extensive appendix cross-referencing.

Limitations are only briefly acknowledged (BT-model alternative not provided, small-scale experiments) without discussing the more fundamental concern that the theoretical 'dichotomy' may not predict real-world behavior beyond the specific constructed counterexamples.

strengths: Provides a comprehensive and fine-grained theoretical taxonomy of RLHF vs. DPO performance gaps, systematically removing the realizability assumption that dominates prior theoretical work, and covering policy-only, reward-only, double, and isomorphic mis-specification regimes with matching propositions and constructive counterexamples for each case.

The statistical-efficiency analysis (Section 4) is a genuinely novel contribution: by introducing a token-level linear parameterization and a dual-token sparse prediction (DTSP) task, the paper rigorously separates the sample complexity of pure reward learning (O(k log d/n)) from DPO's implicit reward learning (Ω(d/n)), giving a concrete mechanism for why RLHF can be more sample-efficient despite both methods sharing realizability.

Strong engagement with and extension of the two most relevant prior works (Nika et al. 2024; Swamy et al. 2026), with explicit, itemized clarification of what is new (regularized metric, finer-grained mis-specification analysis, improved/sharper statistical rates).

Theoretical claims are corroborated both by small controlled experiments on GPT-2-Large/PKU-SafeRLHF that qualitatively match each proposition, and by an extensive, well-organized mapping of the theoretical predictions onto findings from several independent large-scale empirical studies (Table/figure citations from Xu et al. 2024b, Ivison et al. 2024, Razin et al. 2026b, Swamy et al. 2026, Rafailov et al. 2023), which substantially strengthens external validity despite the small-scale own experiments.

The 'bonus' appendix section offering a principled explanation for the PILAF sampler and a bridge to alternative (IPO-style) preference modeling objectives adds practical value beyond the core theory.
Honest and appropriately scoped limitations section; proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: Many of the separating constructions (e.g., 3-action bandits with hand-crafted feature maps) are minimal existence proofs rather than demonstrations of how often or how severely these effects occur in realistic settings; the paper does not quantify the 'size' of the gap as a function of natural problem parameters beyond the DTSP sparsity example.

Empirical verification is conducted only on a single small base model (GPT-2-Large, 774M) and a single dataset (PKU-SafeRLHF), which is a meaningful limitation for claims about practical relevance to modern LLM-scale RLHF/DPO pipelines; this is acknowledged but still constrains confidence in the practical magnitude of the predicted effects.

The main exact-optimization results (Table 1), while rigorously derived, are largely consistent with intuitive expectations (RLHF favored when reward is realizable/policy misspecified and vice versa for DPO); the main value added is formal rigor rather than new qualitative insight, and the double-mis-specification 'no consistent gap' result, while honest, is less conclusive than the other cases.

The negative result that online DPO (even with the PILAF sampler) cannot close the gap under policy mis-specification is demonstrated only for the specific PILAF sampling scheme; it is unclear how robust this conclusion is to other online/exploration strategies not considered in the paper.

The paper's generalization claims from the single-/dual-token linear setting to general multi-token, nonlinear LLM policies rely on intuition ('our intuition... holds for all parameterizations and multi-token cases') rather than formal proof, which is explicitly acknowledged but leaves a gap between the rigorous core theorems and the broader narrative the paper builds around them.

The large number of propositions/conditions, while thorough, makes the exposition dense and taxonomic; a reader must track many conditions (1-7) and their interactions, which could be streamlined for clarity.
